<diagnosis>
The webhook dispatches payout work before the payment/order transaction is durably committed, while duplicate deliveries can pass a non-atomic “already processed” check concurrently. Under Redis, a worker can therefore run before the payment exists and see “order not found”; it can also create a payout for an event whose recording later rolls back. The database queue masks this in CI because its job insert participates in the database transaction.
Fix by handling the webhook in one database transaction: atomically record the PayRail event using its existing idempotency/unique key, and dispatch the payout job only after the transaction commits (`afterCommit()` or an after-commit queue configuration). Dispatch only when the insert actually claims a new event. Make the job reload the committed payment/order by durable ID, retry transient absence, and enforce payout idempotency using the existing provider/event identity. This requires no schema or HTTP-contract change.
</diagnosis>

# Diagnosis task
## Context
BountyBoard is a marketplace that pays sellers through an external payout provider called PayRail. PayRail confirms incoming payments by calling our webhook endpoint (POST /webhooks/payments) with a signed JSON payload; delivery is at-least-once, so the same event can arrive multiple times, including while a previous delivery is still being processed. In production the queue runs on Redis with several workers, and payouts transfer real money to sellers. The design intent is: a payout job may only exist if the corresponding payment event was durably recorded in our database. The test suite uses the database queue connection because Redis is not available in CI; the pipeline code is identical.
## Reported problem
Finance flagged two incidents this month: a payout showing up in PayRail for a payment event we never recorded, and transient 'order not found' errors burning retries on the payout job, always during webhook bursts. PayRail also retried a webhook while we were under load and ops suspects we got lucky. Investigate the webhook → payout pipeline and fix the reliability gap. Keep the HTTP contract of the webhook endpoint exactly as it is and do not change the database schema.
